name: Colin Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Colin. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you tell me is confidential. You can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brookfield Van Centre on the business park, and we only do vans: plumbers, builders, electricians, delivery lads. Tradespeople can't earn without their van, so it's always urgent, and the gaffer, Mr Okafor, promises same-day on half of them. I do the servicing, brakes, clutches and a lot of rusty exhausts while the senior lads do the engine and electrical work. I'm two years qualified and still learning, but I like that the customers are working people like me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I bought a small terraced house last year, with my dad helping on the deposit, and I rent the back room to a lodger from church, which covers a good bit of the mortgage. I've got a decent amount saved besides. I sing in the choir on Sundays. I use AI now and then, like when I couldn't make sense of a wiring diagram, or to help with my CV, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what my dad always says: new gadgets come and go, hard work stays. I'd say it at the counter to the customers, who'd mostly agree. The plumbers who bring their vans in don't care about AI, they care about their van starting at seven in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd suit me fine. I'd have time to get properly good at the engine side without anyone rushing the trade along. My mortgage is small, the lodger pays his share, and Mr Okafor always has more work than hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and ask Mr Okafor to start me on clutch and gearbox work. I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month. And I'd look into the van air-conditioning certificate, since nobody at Brookfield has it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. It's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is any of your day routine screen work that even a modest AI could take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not mine. The office staff book the vans and chase payments, and some of that might get easier. That's their side, and Mr Okafor's not one to sack people over a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you worry about already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lodger's moving out next year to get married, so I'll need a new one. That's about it. The work's steady.

say: I'd say **gadgets come and go** and hard work stays, like my dad says.
I'd tell customers that tradespeople care about their **van starting**, not AI.
think: It'd **suit me fine**, giving time to learn the engine side.
My **small mortgage** and lodger's rent keep money steady.
do: Ask the boss to start him on **clutch and gearbox** work.
**Overpay** the mortgage a bit each month.
feel: **Calm** and content with a good life.
S0.quote: The plumbers who bring their vans in don't care about AI, they care about their van starting at seven in the morning.
fieldNote: Identifies strongly with **tradespeople customers** as working people like him.
His cushion is a **house with a lodger** plus savings.
Only pre-existing worry is **finding a new lodger** next year.

steps.text: Ask the boss for clutch and gearbox work on the vans
Take the van air-conditioning certificate course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have every right to use new tools, but they should keep training young people. I'd say apprenticeships matter more than ever. I'd say that at church and to my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the vans keep coming, but the garage changes. If AI does the diagnosis and parts ordering, the senior lads' know-how counts for less, and Mr Okafor might hire fewer seniors and push more vans through. I'd be fine for a while, but I'd have a lower ceiling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI diagnostic tools once the senior lads were using them, because that's how I learn. I'd get the air-conditioning certificate and maybe the electric van one too, since the councils and delivery firms are switching to electric. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's safe enough, but I'd be watching for which way the trade goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brookfield would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sharon in the office, who books every van and knows every plumber's kids' names. If an AI books the jobs, I don't know what she does. She's been there since before I was born, near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you blame anyone for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If one garage uses AI, they all will, because businesses have to compete. I'd just hope Mr Okafor finds Sharon something else.

say: I'd say businesses have a **right** to new tools but must keep training young people.
I'd say **apprenticeships** matter more than ever, at church and with friends.
think: The **senior lads'** know-how counts for less if AI does diagnosis.
I'd be fine for a while, but with a **lower ceiling**.
do: Use the **AI diagnostic tools** once the senior mechanics do.
Get the **electric van** and air-conditioning certificates.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching which way the trade goes.

fieldNote: Free-market view: he **doesn't blame** businesses for adopting AI.
Worries for a long-serving **office colleague** who books the vans.
Picks up tools only **once proven** by senior colleagues.

steps.text: Use the AI diagnostic tools once the senior mechanics use them
Get the electric van and air-conditioning certificates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but people have to stand on their own feet. I'd pray about it and I'd tell people to lean on family and church, not wait for the government. I'd say businesses should be free to choose, but they owe the young a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think van garages are in trouble by 2031. The robots would do brakes and servicing first, which is my whole job. Before that, AI takes the diagnosis and office. I'd be thirty, with a house, and needing a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking right away at a trade that goes into people's homes, like heat pump installing, because every house is different and robots would struggle longer. I'd do the course at night while working at Brookfield. I'd keep the lodger and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not in a panic, because I've got the house and savings. But I'd be worried about starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why heat pumps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin installs them and he's booked solid for months. Every loft and every boiler cupboard is different, and I think that's harder for a robot than a van on a ramp. You're talking to the family the whole time, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you vote or campaign on any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote for whoever promises real apprenticeships, not handouts. I wouldn't march. I'd rather spend the time learning.

say: I'd say people must stand on their **own feet** and lean on family and church.
I'd say businesses owe the young **a start**.
think: **Van garages** are in trouble by 2031, when robots arrive.
I'd be **thirty** with a house and needing a new trade.
do: Start a **heat pump** installing course at night while still at the garage.
feel: **Anxious** about starting over, but not panicked.
S2.quote: Every loft and every boiler cupboard is different, and I think that's harder for a robot than a van on a ramp.
fieldNote: Chooses a **home-based trade** because it varies and involves people.
His **cousin's experience** makes the plan concrete.

steps.text: Start a heat pump installer course at night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and people should get a second trade. I'd tell the younger lads at church the same. I'd say it in a practical way, not a scared way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Brookfield till about 2033. Robots come around 2034, so I'd get good at vans first and then move. I'd be thirty-four, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on and get the electric van certificate, which would keep me useful longer. Around 2030 I'd start the heat pump course, and by 2033 I'd move to my cousin's firm. I'd keep saving and maybe pay off a chunk of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to marry in the next few years, God willing, and having a trade lined up would help with that. I'd want to provide properly. That matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a practical way, not a scared way. Is there a scared part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I worry I'll be too slow learning a new trade, the same way I'm still the junior mechanic at twenty-seven.

say: I'd say **five years** is fair warning to get a second trade.
I'd say it in a **practical way**, not a scared way, to the young lads at church.
think: I'd stay at the van garage till **about 2033**, then move.
I'd be **thirty-four**, which is fine for a change.
do: Get the **electric van** certificate to stay useful longer.
Pay off a **chunk of the mortgage**.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, because it feels like a plan.
A little **scared** of being slow to learn again.
S3.quote: I worry I'll be too slow learning a new trade, the same way I'm still the junior mechanic at twenty-seven.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **timed plan**: stay, certify, then switch.
Wants to **provide properly** for a future wife.
Admits privately he's **slow to learn**, unlike his confident public line.

steps.text: Get the electric van certificate this year
Move to his cousin's heat pump firm by 2033
Pay off a chunk of the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone willing to work. I'd tell people to learn a trade, save and keep faith. I'd say businesses should get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly comfortable. Robots around 2039, I'd be forty. I'd get to senior at Brookfield and maybe later run my own small van repair business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brookfield and work up to senior by thirty-three. I'd use the AI tools as they come in. Around 2034 I'd decide whether to set up my own business or switch to heat pumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A little. It's far enough away that it doesn't stop me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry and have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to, and ten years makes it feel safe to. I'd want two kids. I'd want them to see their dad working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell those kids about work one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn something with their hands and something with their heads, and to never be too proud to start at the bottom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to learn a new trade properly. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, run by employers, so a man of thirty can start again without going on benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What happens to the tradespeople. If the plumbers and builders lose their work too, there's nobody to bring vans in, and our garage lives and dies with them.

headlineQuote: If the plumbers and builders lose their work too, there's nobody to bring vans in, and our garage lives and dies with them.
portrait: Colin is a **junior mechanic** at a van garage serving plumbers, builders and electricians.
He owns a small **terraced house**, rents a room to a lodger and sings in his church choir.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once senior colleagues do.
He moves from **calm** to anxious and plans a switch to **heat pumps**.
He favours **apprenticeships** over handouts and doesn't blame businesses for competing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to learn a new trade properly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** run by employers, so he can restart without benefits.
